pages.title: How to use this
pages.lede: Everything needed to take a Client from signed to launched, plus the reference tables you will want open while you work.

blocks.title: Two ways to read this
blocks.content:
This manual replaces the three separate documents that came before it. It is built for two different moments, and it is worth knowing which one you are in.

Reading it through: work sections 01 through 13 in order during your first week. Part A explains why the system works, which matters more than it sounds — most launch mistakes come from someone executing a step correctly without understanding what it is for. Part B is the build. Part C is how we read performance once ads are live.

Grabbing something mid-launch: use Settings lookup when you need one exact value and you have a Client on the phone. Use the Launch runsheet as a live checklist on launch day. Section numbers are stable, so "check 09.4" is a valid thing to say to a colleague.
blocks.caveatLabel: The one idea to hold onto
blocks.caveat: The build is not the hard part. A funnel takes about three minutes once you have a snapshot. What separates a launch that works from one that burns a Client's budget is settings discipline in Meta and the quality of the callout. Everything else is assembly.

blocks.title: Before you train anyone from this
blocks.content: The Open items section lists practices that appear in the source recordings but need a decision from leadership before they go into anyone's training. Two of them carry real exposure. Read that section before you pass this manual to a new hire.

pages.title: What we actually sell
pages.lede: Not ads. Not a funnel. A client acquisition system built for a market that is skeptical, informed, and outcome-driven.

blocks.title: One niche, calibrated benchmarks
blocks.content: TAG is niched entirely to the accounting world. Every Client is an accounting firm, and the repositioning work described in section 02 always runs in one direction: from compliance work toward tax advisory as the differentiator. That specificity is what makes the rest of the system work. The messaging patterns, the funnel models, and the cost-per-call benchmarks are all calibrated against this one niche.

blocks.title: §01.1 The five jobs
rows: Reposition compliance work as advisory. Section 02.
Test angles, hooks, and callouts until one converts. We own this, not the Client.
Repeat a known-good configuration as far as the Client's capacity allows.

blocks.content: Results from this don't grow linearly. Until the message is cracked, performance looks flat or noisy. Once it lands, sales accelerate quickly because the rest of the system was already built and waiting.

blocks.title: Why this framing matters on calls
blocks.content: Clients who think they bought ads will judge you on ad metrics from day one. Clients who understand they bought a system will give the messaging phase the room it needs. Set this expectation during onboarding, not after a slow first week.

pages.title: Offer conversion
pages.lede: The most important part of the system, and the first thing you should be able to explain to a Client.

blocks.title: §02.1 Why compliance-only stopped working
blocks.content:
An accounting firm selling pure compliance — bookkeeping, tax prep, filing — is running out of room. The market is saturated with commodity firms, buyers have been burned by firms that just do the numbers with no strategic input, and clients increasingly expect more than historical reporting.

Standing out on compliance alone requires a strong personal brand, heavy trust upfront, and long nurturing cycles. Most Clients don't have that and don't need it.

blocks.title: §02.2 Compliance becomes advisory
blocks.content:
We convert the Client's offer from compliance-based accounting to advisory-based service, specifically tax advisory. We don't sell bookkeeping and filing as the headline. We sell the tax strategy and the savings outcome.

What changes: the Client takes on strategic ownership, the offer reads as higher value, the buying decision gets easier, price resistance drops, and they stop competing on hourly rates against every other firm in their market.

rows: "We'll handle your bookkeeping and file your taxes on time."
"A done-for-you tax advisory engagement where we restructure your finances to legally minimize what you owe, so more of what you make stays with you."

blocks.content: Same firm. Same underlying work. Different packaging, higher perceived value, more visible results, better margins per engagement. The positioning is the difference, not the accounting.

blocks.title: §02.3 Why advisory converts cold traffic
blocks.content:
Advisory offers don't require blind trust. They deliver something tangible — a strategy, a savings number, a plan — and they shift execution risk off the buyer. Trust gets built through clear process, defined outcomes, strong positioning, and risk reversal, rather than through personal brand or social proof alone.

That's why these offers survive cold traffic, support higher ad spend, and scale faster than a generic "we do your books" pitch.

blocks.title: Guardrail
blocks.content: Repositioning affects what a Client is allowed to claim. Our Clients are licensed practitioners. Section 09.6 covers what can and cannot go into a guarantee — read it before writing any advisory copy.

blocks.title: §02.4 Financing
blocks.content: We help Clients connect financing options for their own clients. This lowers friction, raises close rates, and improves cash flow, because buyers evaluate monthly affordability rather than total price.

pages.lede: You should be able to run this math live on a call without notes.

blocks.title: The reframe that closes Clients
blocks.content: A $2,000 CAC on a $10,000 client is not $2,000 lost. It's $2,000 deployed to buy $10,000. Once that holds, the only remaining question is how many times it can be repeated — and the answer should be: as many times as the business can handle. That's scaling.

blocks.title: §03.1 Why high ticket wins with paid ads
blocks.content:
Ads carry fixed costs, and low-ticket offers break under that pressure. High-ticket offers absorb CAC, fund aggressive testing, scale faster, outbid competitors, and leave more net profit.

Once CAC and ROAS are known, spend becomes predictable, risk becomes calculated, and growth becomes a decision rather than a gamble. Ads stop feeling risky and start functioning as leverage.

pages.title: Funnel models
pages.lede: Three variations. Which one a Client gets depends on their offer, price point, and team.

blocks.title: §04.1 Direct application to call booking
blocks.content:
Flow: Ads → VSL → Application → Booked call

Best for high-ticket offers, owner-led sales, lower volume at higher quality. Prioritizes intent, efficiency, and qualified conversations. This is the default build described in sections 07 through 09.

blocks.title: §04.2 Application plus setter follow-up
blocks.content:
Flow: Ads → VSL → Application, then a setter calls everyone who didn't book, qualifies them, and books the call.

Best for higher lead volume, accounts leaking missed bookings, and growing sales teams. Raises booking rate, improves ROAS, and gets more out of the same ad spend.

blocks.title: §04.3 Live transfer
blocks.content:
Flow: Lead opts in → setter calls immediately → qualifies in real time → live transfer into Zoom or Google Meet → Client or rep closes while intent is highest.

Best for aggressive scaling, speed-sensitive offers, and high daily spend. Speed is the whole mechanism here.

rows: Setter and closer available on demand

pages.title: Pre-launch gate
pages.lede: Missing Client assets are the most common cause of a stalled launch. Chasing them mid-build wastes hours.

blocks.title: How "Ad account access granted" actually works (updated 2026-08-19)
blocks.content:
We do not use Meta Business Manager Partner (business-to-business) sharing — no Client is Partner-connected to TAG's Business Manager, and none will be. Access works in two steps instead:

1. The Client adds support@taxadvisorygrowth.net as a Business Manager Admin — Business Settings → Users → People → Add. It must be full Business Manager Admin, not just Advertiser/Admin access scoped to one ad account. That single step is the entire Client-side ask.
2. From that login, TAG creates a System User inside the Client's own Business Manager, installs TAG's app (tag-hub-server) if it isn't already selectable, assigns the Client's ad account and pixel to the System User, and generates the access token the Hub app uses for automated spend/ROAS/campaign management. The Client never touches Meta's System User settings.

Don't ask a Client to create a System User themselves or to grant access to a TAG-owned one that already exists — both of those assume a Partner relationship, which we deliberately don't use. Before checking this row done, confirm the grant was Business Manager Admin, not ad-account-level Advertiser access — Advertiser-only access doesn't expose System Users at all, and you'll hit a dead end mid-build.

blocks.title: If the pre-call video isn't filmed
blocks.content: Don't hold the launch for it. Clone the step, strip the video block, replace it with a short thank-you headline, and publish it as a plain thank-you page. Swap the real video in when it arrives. A Client waiting on their own asset shouldn't cost them a week of spend.

pages.title: Asset scripting
pages.lede: Scripting the VSL, the ad, and the pre-call video with ChatGPT.

blocks.title: One asset at a time
steps: Script each asset as a separate prompt in a separate pass. Batching all three into one request reliably produces worse output — the structure flattens and the results need more rework than the time you saved.

blocks.title: The modeling prompt
steps: Copy the entire completed intake form.
Paste into ChatGPT with: "Rewrite this, modeling the exact structure of the text I am about to send you."
Wait for it to confirm, then send the proven template for that asset type.
Iterate: feed in the unique mechanism, tighten the callout, make it more assertive, name the specific audience.
blocks.note: This works because output is modeled on structures already proven in market rather than generated from scratch.

blocks.title: Headline pattern
steps: Three components: an attention statement naming a specific audience, the guarantee, and an aggressive offer paired with an aggressive guarantee. If ChatGPT drifts, give it a direct example in that format rather than describing what you want.

blocks.title: Check before it goes in the builder
blocks.content: Copy is ready when it names a specific audience, states the guarantee, and reflects the Client's approved unique mechanism. Copy written against an unconverted offer — see section 02 — will underperform no matter how good the media buying is.

blocks.title: Wistia upload standard
steps: Naming. Label the video with the client's business name, not a generic label like "call" or "VSL." This is what keeps the shared Wistia account navigable as the client list grows.

Color code. Go to Appearances and set the player color to the team's standard code (editor's reference is yellow). We pay for Wistia specifically to get branded, trackable players — an unbranded default-blue player defeats the point of the paid account.
Thumbnail. Actually pick one. Don't accept a black frame or a frame that's just floating text. Pick a frame that looks presentable at a glance.
Controls — turn on: Auto Play, Play with Sound, Big Play Button, Full Screen.
Controls — turn off: Control Bar, Play Bar, Captions, Settings.
blocks.note: Why Captions is off: The editor already burns captions into the creative itself. Leaving Wistia's native captions on stacks a second, unstyled caption layer on top of the editor's — turn it off every time.

pages.title: Funnel build
pages.lede: Three pages in GoHighLevel. Roughly three minutes once you have a snapshot.

blocks.title: Do this once, save it forever
blocks.content: After your first clean build, take a snapshot and deploy every subsequent funnel from it. This is the single biggest time saver available to you.

blocks.title: Create the shell
steps: Sites → Funnels → New Funnel, name it, build from scratch.
Add the first step, name the page VSL, path /VSL.
Connect the Client's domain.

blocks.title: VSL page
steps: Headline — attention statement naming the audience. Size 21, heavy.
Headline — guarantee and offer. Size 39, 900 heavy.
Video — set type to Custom Embed, paste the Wistia embed code.
Button — "Schedule a Free Demo", subtext "Limited spots available." Sizes 22 and 15, heavy then bold. Link to next step. Background #EBC507, black text.
Headline — disclaimer, rewritten for the Client. Size 12, with spacing above.
Save, or confirm autosave is on.

blocks.title: Mobile sizing — before you clone
steps: Switch to Mobile mode on the VSL page.
Headline 1 → 14. Headline 2 → 16.
Button → unchanged. Disclaimer → 8.
Now clone, and mobile settings carry through.
blocks.warning: Do this on step one before cloning anything. Mobile layout does not carry over once you've already cloned. Fixing it afterward means redoing every step by hand.

blocks.title: Application page
steps: Clone Funnel Step from VSL. Rename immediately: step name "App", path /app. Update the step.
Rewrite the top headline via ChatGPT to close the loop. Size stays 39.
Delete the original headline and the button. Keep the disclaimer.
Add Calendar, select the Client's GoHighLevel calendar, set redirect to "Go to Next Step."
Add an underlined line above it, e.g. "Schedule a strategy call", with a blank spacer.

blocks.title: Pre-call page
steps: Clone Funnel Step from Application. Rename to "Pre-Call", path /ty.
Replace the headline: "Important — after adding the event to your calendar, watch the video below so we can hit the ground running on your call." Size 20.
Delete the calendar element.
Add Video, Custom Embed, for the pre-call video.
Add a second headline: "Add the event to your calendar — go to your email and click Add to Calendar." Size 23, bold.

blocks.title: Rename before you edit
blocks.content: Cloned steps keep the word "clone" in the name and inherit the wrong path. Rename and update the path immediately after cloning, before touching content. Leftover clone names in a live URL are visible to the Client's prospects.

pages.title: Pixel install
pages.lede: The step most likely to be done wrong. When it's wrong, the campaign optimizes against nothing and the spend is wasted silently.

blocks.title: Non-obvious requirement
blocks.content: Create the data set from inside the ad account — not from Events Manager, not from Business Settings. Created elsewhere, it won't appear correctly as a selectable option in the campaign.

blocks.title: Create the data set
steps: In Ads Manager at ad set level, under Data Set, choose Create Data Set.
Name it after the Client's company. Keep it simple.
Select Meta Pixel only, not Conversions API.
Choose Install code manually, then copy the code.

blocks.title: Install in GoHighLevel
steps: Funnel → Settings.
Paste into Head Tracking Code. Not Body Tracking Code. This is a silent failure that costs days.
Scroll to the bottom and save. Allow a minute to propagate.

blocks.title: Map the conversion event
steps: Back in Events Manager, hit Continue. Leave the toggle Meta offers off.
Add Events → paste the full VSL page URL → continue. Meta loads the live page.
Use Track Button, not URL tracking. Click the schedule button on the loaded page.
Map it to the standard event Schedule. Confirm.
Finish setup → Finish → Skip → Done.

blocks.title: Verify before you spend
steps: Return to Ads Manager and refresh. The data set should now be selectable.
Set conversion event to Schedule. It will show "no data" — expected on a fresh pixel.
Run a test booking through the live funnel and confirm the event fires in Test Events.
Use the standard TAG test record. Never personal contact details.
If events don't appear: re-copy the pixel code, delete the old code from Head Tracking, paste fresh, save, retest. Propagation delay is common — wait a minute before assuming failure.

blocks.content:
Everything else is unselected. The rest is treated as wasted spend.

Facebook: Feed, Stories, Reels

blocks.title: Audience Network re-toggles itself
blocks.content: After you switch it off, Meta frequently turns it back on when you change another setting. Turn it off, then check it again immediately before you publish. Same applies to multi-advertiser ads.

blocks.title: §09.3 Starting budgets
blocks.content:
Constrained budget floor: $50/day — Workable with one creative, slower to signal
Standard recommendation: $100/day — Reaches a decision point in 1–3 days
Three or more creatives: $100–150/day — Bump so each creative gets data
Aggressive first launch: $150–200/day — Where the Client's budget supports it
Iteration 2 audience split: ~$25/day each — e.g. four callout variants at $25

Faster spend produces faster clarity. A Client at $100/day reaches a working configuration meaningfully sooner than one at $50/day — worth saying out loud when they're deciding.

blocks.title: §09.4 Ad copy structure
blocks.content:
1. Callout — name the exact person. "Business owners earning $500K+ only."
2. Offer and guarantee — the outcome plus the risk reversal.
3. CTA — "Click the link below to book your strategy call."

The callout also does targeting work. Because detailed targeting is left open, the copy is the primary signal telling Meta who should see this ad. That's why we test the callout and leave the targeting alone.

blocks.title: Be specific, not generic
blocks.content: "High income attorneys" is weak. "Attorneys making over $400,000 a year" is the callout. The more specific the income or role qualifier in the copy, the tighter the audience Meta delivers to — vague callouts pull in browsers, specific ones pull in the Client's actual buyer.

blocks.title: §09.5 Creative handling
blocks.content:
- Editor delivers assets. Clients request revisions directly in the editing tool rather than routing through you.
- Default is one ad, modeled on a proven template. More only when the Client wants aggression and can fund it.
- Set thumbnails manually. Auto-selected frames are frequently unflattering. No measured performance impact, but it affects how the Client perceives the work.
- Publishing multiple ads may require publishing each one individually.

blocks.title: Guarantee language
blocks.content:
Source material includes a guarantee promising to reduce tax liability by a specific large percentage or refund. That carries two risks. The first is Meta rejection, which is recoverable. The second is not: our Clients are licensed accountants and CPAs governed by IRS Circular 230, state board advertising rules, and AICPA conduct standards. An ad guaranteeing a specific tax outcome can create licensure exposure for the Client — a far worse failure than a rejected ad.

Standard: no specific percentage or dollar tax-savings guarantee without written sign-off from the Client's licensed practitioner. Guarantee the process and the engagement, not the number.

pages.title: Reminder automations
pages.lede: Built in GoHighLevel Workflows. Reduces no-shows, which directly protects cost per held call.

blocks.title: Configuration overview
rows: Calendar equals the specific strategy session calendar
Until Scheduled Time → Appointment Time → X hours before
SMS and email at every interval
The Client's own address, verified before building

blocks.title: §10.1 Custom values to insert
blocks.content:
- Contact → Full Name
- Appointment → Start Date and Time
- Appointment → Meeting Location

Paste operations frequently drop or mangle these tokens. Re-insert from the Custom Values menu rather than typing them, and read every message before enabling the workflow.

blocks.title: Why both channels every time
blocks.content:
If A2P 10DLC registration isn't approved, SMS won't deliver and a text-only sequence fails silently — the Client sees no-shows and no explanation. Email duplication means reminder coverage works on day one regardless.

Note: the founder calls this "HTTP" in the recordings. The actual item is A2P 10DLC carrier registration. Search that term, not the other one.

blocks.title: Trigger and calendar
steps: Trigger: Customer Booked Appointment. No extra trigger filters needed beyond the calendar itself.
Name the calendar after the Client's business, never the personal calendar GoHighLevel creates by default — e.g. [Firm Name] Tax Strategy Assessment Call.
Add the Client's logo to the calendar. Small effort, visibly raises perceived quality.
Name the workflow itself after the client, e.g. TAG Reminders or [Firm Name] Reminders.

blocks.title: Immediate confirmation — SMS and email
steps: Build the SMS action first, then the email action directly beneath it in the same workflow step.

blocks.title: Wait steps and the reminder cadence
steps: After the immediate confirmation, insert a Wait step: Until Scheduled Time → Appointment Time → 12 hours before, with Skip all outbound communications until the next one selected. Repeat this wait-then-send pattern for each interval.

blocks.title: Token discipline
blocks.content: Always re-insert {{contact.name}}, {{appointment.start_time}}, and {{appointment.meeting_location}} from the Custom Values menu rather than typing or pasting them — paste operations frequently mangle the braces. Read every message in the workflow before turning it on.

blocks.title: If A2P isn't approved yet
blocks.content: Run every one of these as email-only until approval comes through. Same cadence, same copy, drop the SMS actions.

pages.title: Qualification and DQ
pages.lede: Stopping unqualified prospects from consuming the Client's calendar.

blocks.title: §11.1 Form fields
blocks.content:
A strong reference set from a live tax advisory Client:

- Name, email, phone number
- Company website
- States taxed in
- Industry
- Services of interest — tax reduction, preparation, accounting, other
- Estimated net taxable income, current year, business + personal
- Estimated revenue, current year

The income and revenue fields are what the conditional logic keys off. Build the form with the Client on their launch call. Use a single Full Name field rather than splitting first and last, and include the consent checkbox for text messages.

blocks.title: §11.2 DQ page and routing
blocks.content:
1. Clone an existing funnel step, rename to DQ, update the path.
2. Strip it to a short headline. Keep the tone professional — this page still represents the Client to someone who may qualify later.
3. Optional: a "what happens next" paragraph with resources, and a closing appreciation line.
4. Publish and copy the URL.
5. In the form, open conditional logic on the income field: if under threshold, redirect to the DQ URL.
6. Alternative: display an inline custom message instead of redirecting. Faster to build, less polished.

Test the logic end to end with a dummy under-threshold submission before go-live.

blocks.title: Set expectations on this
blocks.content: Raising the qualification bar raises cost per booked call, because you're filtering more traffic out. That's expected and is not a signal the campaign is failing. Agree the threshold with the Client explicitly so the resulting number isn't a surprise in week one.

pages.title: KPIs
pages.lede: What good looks like, and how quickly you can tell.

rows: Under $80 is strong. $32–60 observed on healthy accounts.
At $100/day, enough signal to decide the next move

blocks.title: Rising cost per call isn't automatically a problem
blocks.content: One reference account opened around $37 and settled higher while staying well inside target. Judge against the threshold, not against the opening number. Drift upward over time is normal.

pages.title: Iteration
pages.lede: What to change, in what order, and what to leave alone.

rows: Open targeting, one creative, single callout
Establish a baseline and let Meta find the audience
Split the callout into separate ad sets by segment
Isolate which audience the copy actually converts
Creative variation against the winning callout
Only once the audience is known
Use when lead quality is poor, as a test — not a default

blocks.title: The operating principle
blocks.content: We test copy, not targeting. The assumption is that Meta's delivery optimization outperforms manual audience construction, so the lever we pull is the callout. If a Client's ad names five different audiences at once, that's a signal to split it into a proper test rather than a finished ad.

blocks.title: §13.1 Worked example
blocks.content: An ad calling out executives, leaders, CEOs, and doctors simultaneously isn't one ad — it's four untested hypotheses in a trench coat. Iteration 2 for that account is four ad sets at $25/day, each naming one audience, running the same three creatives. Within a few days you know which callout carries the account, and iteration 3 puts full budget behind it.

blocks.title: §13.2 Efficiency notes
blocks.content:
- Build a snapshot and deploy every funnel from it.
- Clone, don't build. Every additional step should be a clone, stripped and edited.
- Set mobile sizing before cloning. See 07.3.
- Add the Client's logo to calendar settings. Quick, and visibly raises perceived quality.
- Cap the booking window at 5–7 days. Longer windows produce cold, low-show bookings.
